Parallel contributions—Effective Program Debloating via Reinforcement Learning (2018) and Charting the Attack Surface of Trigger-Action IoT Platforms (2019) —reinforced the foundational challenges in this space.

A productive wave of CCS work from 2020–2022 deepened the area. PDiff: Semantic-based Patch Presence Testing for Downstream Kernels (CCS 2020) advanced the field by demonstrating PDiff uses semantic analysis to test whether downstream kernels have applied security patches from mainline. Other strong contributions included Logging to the Danger Zone: Race Condition Attacks and Defenses on System Audit Frameworks (2020), NARRATOR: Secure and Practical State Continuity for Trusted Execution in the Cloud (2022), broadening the space of techniques and targets.

The most recent CCS contributions (from 2023 onward) reflect a maturing field that pushes into harder targets and broader threat models. Are we there yet? An Industrial Viewpoint on Provenance-based Endpoint Detection and Response Tools (CCS 2023) exemplified this trend by tackling Industrial evaluation of provenance-based endpoint detection and response tools for APT defense. Similarly, SyzDirect: Directed Greybox Fuzzing for Linux Kernel (2023) and Greybox Fuzzing of Distributed Systems (2023) show how the community continues to scale and adapt its methods.

uss.narrative:
The earliest cluster here (USENIX 2018) shows OS and systems security split between two fronts: hardening the kernel attack surface and reasoning about attacks after they happen. On the offensive/defensive boundary, "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018) was the watershed, demonstrating that microarchitectural side effects could shatter the most basic assumption of OS security, that the kernel address space is isolated from user space. Around it, a wave of kernel-fuzzing and exploitation work appeared: "MoonShine: Optimizing OS Fuzzer Seed Selection with Trace Distillation" (USENIX 2018) made syscall fuzzing smarter, while "FUZE: Towards Facilitating Exploit Generation for Kernel Use-After-Free Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2018) pushed toward automatically judging which kernel bugs are actually exploitable. A parallel thread tackled bloat and isolation at the software level, with "Debloating Software through Piece-Wise Compilation and Loading" (USENIX 2018) and "Security Namespace: Making Linux Security Frameworks Available to Containers" (USENIX 2018), alongside provenance-and-forensics systems like "SAQL" and "Dependence-Preserving Data Compaction for Scalable Forensic Analysis" (both USENIX 2018) aimed at investigating long-running APT campaigns.

By 2019-2020 the field's center of gravity shifted toward fine-grained, in-process isolation, partly as a response to both Spectre/Meltdown-class leaks and the desire for least privilege without full process separation. "ERIM: Secure, Efficient In-process Isolation with Protection Keys (MPK)" (USENIX 2019) showed that Intel MPK could give cheap intra-process compartments, and "Donky" (USENIX 2020) extended that idea to RISC-V and x86. The community then immediately stress-tested the approach: "PKU Pitfalls: Attacks on PKU-based Memory Isolation Systems" (USENIX 2020) exposed real weaknesses in PKU-based schemes, a healthy attack-defense loop. In the browser, "Site Isolation: Process Separation for Web Sites within the Browser" (USENIX 2019) brought the same isolation philosophy to web origins. Meanwhile attack-surface reduction matured from static debloating ("RAZOR", USENIX 2019) into runtime, phase-aware specialization with "Temporal System Call Specialization for Attack Surface Reduction" (USENIX 2020), and kernel access-control analysis advanced through "PeX: A Permission Check Analysis Framework for Linux Kernel" (USENIX 2019) and missing-check detection.

From 2021 onward the work climbed the stack and got more automated. Fuzzing moved beyond the kernel proper to hypervisors and device interfaces, with "Nyx: Greybox Hypervisor Fuzzing using Fast Snapshots and Affine Types" (USENIX 2021) and earlier "USBFuzz" (USENIX 2020), while "SyzVegas: Beating Kernel Fuzzing Odds with Reinforcement Learning" (USENIX 2021) brought learning-based tuning to fuzzers. Isolation expanded to new runtimes and threat models, including "Swivel: Hardening WebAssembly against Spectre" (USENIX 2021) and automatic least-privilege policy generation for microservices (USENIX 2021). The latest listed work, "PROGRAPHER: An Anomaly Detection System based on Provenance Graph Embedding" (USENIX 2023), shows the forensics thread from 2018 coming full circle, now using graph embeddings and learning to detect APTs rather than just record them. Taken together, the area evolved from foundational isolation breaks and basic kernel fuzzing toward a mature ecosystem of cheap hardware-assisted compartments, automated attack-surface reduction, learning-driven testing, and provenance-based detection.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this list, all from 2018, capture three concerns that would define the area. The most consequential is "Meltdown: Reading Kernel Memory from User Space" (USENIX 2018), which shattered the assumption that hardware memory isolation protects kernel space from user processes, kicking off a wave of microarchitectural-security research. Alongside it, the same year saw a strong push on finding kernel bugs before attackers do, with "MoonShine: Optimizing OS Fuzzer Seed Selection with Trace Distillation" (USENIX 2018) refining system-call fuzzing, and "FUZE: Towards Facilitating Exploit Generation for Kernel Use-After-Free Vulnerabilities" (USENIX 2018) automating exploitability assessment. A parallel thread tackled isolation and attack-surface reduction: "Debloating Software through Piece-Wise Compilation and Loading" (USENIX 2018) and "Effective Program Debloating via Reinforcement Learning" (CCS 2018) cut away unused code, while "Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity" (CCS 2018) tightened CFI defenses.

The second major theme, which quickly grew to dominate this set by citation count, is provenance- and audit-log-based attack detection. Even in 2018, "Towards a Timely Causality Analysis for Enterprise Security" (NDSS 2018) and "SAQL: A Stream-based Query System for Real-Time Abnormal System Behavior Detection" (USENIX 2018) framed intrusion investigation as a problem over system-event graphs, while "Dependence-Preserving Data Compaction for Scalable Forensic Analysis" (USENIX 2018) and "NodeMerge: Template Based Efficient Data Reduction" (CCS 2018) attacked the resulting data-volume problem. In 2019 this matured into real-time APT detection with "HOLMES: Real-Time APT Detection through Correlation of Suspicious Information Flows" (S&P 2019), and confronted the operational pain of false positives in "NoDoze: Combatting Threat Alert Fatigue with Automated Provenance Triage" (NDSS 2019), with "POIROT" (CCS 2019) reframing detection as threat hunting by aligning attack behavior to kernel audit records.

Across 2019-2020 the isolation and fuzzing threads kept advancing in parallel. "ERIM: Secure, Efficient In-process Isolation with Protection Keys (MPK)" (USENIX 2019) showed lightweight intra-process isolation using new hardware primitives, while "SANCTUARY" (NDSS 2019) and the cautionary "SoK: Understanding the Prevailing Security Vulnerabilities in TrustZone-assisted TEE Systems" (S&P 2020) charted both the promise and the fragility of ARM TrustZone enclaves. Kernel bug-finding sharpened around the hard case of concurrency, with "Razzer: Finding Kernel Race Bugs through Fuzzing" (S&P 2019), "HFL: Hybrid Fuzzing on the Linux Kernel" (NDSS 2020), and "Krace: Data Race Fuzzing for Kernel File Systems" (S&P 2020). On detection, "Unicorn: Runtime Provenance-Based Detector for Advanced Persistent Threats" (NDSS 2020) and "Tactical Provenance Analysis for Endpoint Detection and Response Systems" (S&P 2020) pushed graph-based methods toward practical EDR deployment.

The most recent papers show the field consolidating around learning over provenance graphs. "SHADEWATCHER: Recommendation-guided Cyber Threat Analysis" (S&P 2022) borrowed recommendation-system techniques, "PROGRAPHER: An Anomaly Detection System based on Provenance Graph Embedding" (USENIX 2023) leaned on graph embeddings, and "Kairos: Practical Intrusion Detection and Investigation using Whole-system Provenance" (S&P 2024) aimed at practical, whole-system detection and investigation together. Taken as a whole, the area moved from foundational shocks to isolation guarantees (Meltdown, ERIM, TrustZone), through systematic kernel bug discovery (MoonShine, Razzer, HFL, Krace), and converged on increasingly automated, machine-learning-driven analysis of system audit data as the dominant frontier for detecting stealthy, long-running intrusions.
